title: What to Know About Friday’s Nationwide Ground Stop
rawText:
Supported by
What to Know About Friday’s Nationwide Ground Stop
The air traffic control system’s overloaded, antiquated telecommunications equipment sustained its latest widespread failure, prompting a call for more money to fuel faster upgrades.
The Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, after outdated air traffic communications equipment became overloaded with data and began to fail, officials said.
The outage stranded thousands of passengers and caused widespread delays from which airlines and airports are still struggling to recover. It also highlighted persistent vulnerabilities in the aging U.S. air traffic infrastructure and a funding fight, as administration officials demanded lawmakers approve tens of billions of dollars more to accelerate systemwide upgrades.
Here’s what to know.
What caused the problem?
Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, told reporters at the White House Friday night that the radar and other air traffic communications started to falter at 3:36 p.m. when old routers became overloaded with data. While the failures were not universal, they were pervasive enough to prompt officials to issue the unusual nationwide moratorium on takeoffs, Mr. Duffy said.
Appearing alongside him at the White House, Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, stressed that there was no evidence that nefarious activity had triggered the technology failures.
“We’ve seen zero evidence that this was a cyberattack,” Mr. Mullin said, suggesting that new equipment and new technology the Mr. Duffy’s department had added to the old infrastructure was what had overwhelmed it.
Mr. Duffy insisted that the failure was caused by the antiquated, legacy communications equipment, not recent upgrades to the system.

title: U.N. watchdog agency pushes for access to key Iran nuclear site
rawText:
Live Updates: U.N. agency pushes for access to key Iran nuclear site as Trump says deal to end war unnecessary
What to know about the Iran war today:
- The U.N. nuclear watchdog is "increasingly concerned" about Iran refusing its inspectors access to an underground uranium enrichment facility in Isfahan, where highly enriched uranium is thought to be buried, according to Reuters.
- Iran's chief negotiator told Al Jazeera Thursday that U.S. officials asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to facilitate negotiations between Washington and Tehran. The White House has not responded directly to the report.
- "We don't need a deal with Iran," President Trump declared Thursday, ordering Vice President JD Vance to focus on domestic politics instead. Hours earlier, Mr. Trump had again claimed victory in the war, but acknowledged it wasn't over, saying it was "just a question of when we want to end it."
Iran say 2 oil tankers struck mines in Strait of Hormuz
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Saturday that explosions rang out on two oil tankers after they struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz, where Tehran has restricted navigation.
Since war erupted in February, Tehran has insisted that vessels obtain its authorization to cross the strait and has attacked ships that do not comply.
"A short while ago, two oil tankers that had switched off their radar and positioning systems and were secretly attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an unauthorized route exploded and caught fire after striking a naval mine," the Guards' navy said in a statement carried by an Iranian state broadcaster early on Saturday.
The statement did not provide the names or origins of the vessels, but said one was a supertanker.
The U.S., in response to Tehran's choking of the strategic trade route, has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports and provides military support to tankers using the waterway.
In recent weeks, Iran's armed forces have reported several fires or explosions on board ships in the strait, often saying the vessels had struck mines.
On Friday, the Guards released footage of a large plume of smoke rising from a vessel it said was carrying liquefied gas and hit a mine in the south of the strait.
The U.S. military, however, has said it has cleared the main routes through the waterway of mines.
U.N. calls for attacks on civilians in Yemen to stop
U.N. deputy spokesman Farhan Haq said Friday that civilians across Yemen are increasingly being hit by drones, missiles, airstrikes and shelling in their homes, markets and other places once considered safe.
In one of the deadliest attacks since fighting resumed between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and Saudi-backed government forces, at least 30 people died in airstrikes on a market in Taiz province on Nov. 6, according to the Houthis.
Under international law, Haq said all parties must take "all feasible precautions" to avoid and minimize the death and injury to civilians.
Oil prices swing back and forth, wholesale inflation remains high due to diesel costs
Oil prices swung a day after President Trump said the U.S. didn't "need a deal with Iran" even as the conflict in the Middle East drags on.
Brent crude, the international standard, initially jumped early Friday before easing. It was mostly unchanged at $95.89 a barrel at 2 p.m. ET. It was trading near $72 per barrel in late February before the Iran war began.
Rising energy prices because of the U.S. war with Iran have been fueling inflation. Household budgets are getting squeezed directly by higher gasoline costs, but pricier gas and diesel raise costs for anything that is shipped. Prices for everything from food to clothing have been rising.
The latest wholesale inflation report released Friday also shows food prices and other costs gaining ground, despite some easing for energy costs.

title: Nvidia Scandal Prompts Questions of What It Means to Be a Spy
rawText:
Supported by
Nvidia Scandal Prompts Questions of What It Means to Be a Spy
U.S. intelligence agencies believe a woman who had an affair with Jensen Huang was a Chinese asset. But there is much more that they are still assessing about her role.
Alice Huang, the Chinese executive at the center of the Nvidia spying scandal, was believed to be using her affair with Nvidia’s founder to help China get around U.S. efforts to restrict access to advanced A.I. chips, people who have read U.S. intelligence reporting said.
But there remains much that intelligence agencies are still assessing about Ms. Huang including when she began working with China’s top spy agency, whether her cooperation was willing or coerced, how much direction Beijing gave her, and how much she relayed to officials there, the people said.
Her relationship with Jensen Huang, who stepped down as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday, gave her potential access to crucial information about the company’s technology, Mr. Huang’s strategic thinking and his knowledge of Washington’s debates about A.I. policy.
She also had a business interest in ensuring a flow of chips to her own company, one of a number in Southeast Asia that provided Chinese tech firms with the computing power needed to train advanced artificial intelligence models.
The aftershocks of the scandal continue to play out as President Trump prepares for a trip next week to Asia, where he is scheduled to meet with President Xi Jinping of China, who has made a top priority of catching the United States in the race for A.I. dominance.
The unknowns surrounding Ms. Huang have generated intense scrutiny of how Chinese intelligence operates, prompted questions of what it means to be a spy and given backers of Mr. Huang an opening to raise questions about the extent and nature of her role.

title: Trump urge al Congreso a recuperar la producción de Hollywood con incentivos fiscales
rawText:
Los ÁEl presidente de Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, urgió este viernes al Congreso de EE.UU. a sacar adelante un proyecto bipartidista que ofrece incentivos fiscales federales para evitar la fuga de la producción en Hollywood, epicentro de la industria del cine y el entretenimiento del mundo.
En un mensaje en Truth Social, el mandatario explicó que está trabajando con senadores del Partido Republicano y opositores, como el senador demócrata por California Adam Schiff, para que se apruebe la Ley de Revitalización del Cine, la Televisión y el Entretenimiento (Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act), que otorgaría incentivos fiscales a la industria.
Trump subrayó que gran parte de la industria del entretenimiento se ha trasladado a Canadá, el Reino Unido, Australia y otros países; sin embargo, los actores, productores y todos los demás profesionales del sector "¡quieren volver a casa!".
Es importante destacar que cientos de miles de trabajadores se verán beneficiados de manera muy significativa con la aprobación de este proyecto de ley. La inversión destinada a estos incentivos fiscales se recuperará con creces, multiplicada por diez, insistió.
Hollywood sufre desde hace décadas de un fenómeno conocido como 'runaway production': la fuga de las grandes producciones y rodajes de cine o televisión hacia otros países ante la falta de incentivos fiscales atractivos.
Este problema se agravó durante la pandemia de la covid-19, cuando la industria cinematográfica de EE.UU. quedó en una situación de extrema vulnerabilidad y se vivieron las históricas huelgas de guionistas y actores que paralizaron el sector en 2023.
Trump amenazó, en su segunda llegada al poder, con imponer un arancel del 100 % a las películas extranjeras, una medida que generó un fuerte rechazo entre los principales sindicatos y estudios, que advirtieron que paralizaría la distribución global.
En su lugar, los representantes de la industria propusieron una mejora en los créditos fiscales, similares a los que ofrecen países y algunos estados de EE.UU. que se están beneficiando del éxodo de Hollywood, como es el caso de Nuevo México o Georgia.
Esperemos que republicanos y demócratas unan sus fuerzas para finalizar esta legislación, que ya está siendo objeto de intensas negociaciones. Es posible llevarlo a cabo de forma rápida, precisa y eficiente y, lo que es más importante, beneficiará a todo el país, puntualizó el mandatario.

title: Why Anthropic’s Dario Amodei Has Angered OpenAI and Other A.I. Peers
rawText:
Why Silicon Valley’s Knives Came Out for Anthropic
Dario Amodei, the company’s chief executive, publicly frets about the dangers of artificial intelligence and has made enemies of his peers along the way.
Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, was becoming a nuisance for his fellow technology industry executives.
Anthropic and OpenAI, the leading artificial intelligence companies, were lobbying the White House to prevent some A.I. models from being developed and widely shared because, they argued, they were too dangerous. But companies like Nvidia and Microsoft saw those A.I. models as a big business opportunity.
At the end of July, Satya Nadella, chief executive of Microsoft, and Jensen Huang, then Nvidia’s chief executive, intervened. They emailed each other drafts of a letter saying those A.I. models should remain open, according to four people familiar with the discussions. When they asked other technology executives whether they’d like to sign on, two dozen companies quickly agreed before the letter became public. Over the next week, 200 more companies — including a chastened OpenAI — signed onto the letter.
Dr. Amodei refused.
Dr. Amodei has for years exasperated his peers with warnings about extreme risks of A.I., even as his company has built some of the most powerful A.I. systems in the world. Frustration has turned to hostility as Anthropic leaped into the lead in A.I. development, experienced stunning revenue growth and moved toward what is likely to be one of the largest initial public offerings ever later this month.
Along the way, Anthropic — which has cultivated an image as a company that tries to do the right thing — has also gained a reputation for playing hardball with customers and competitors. It has cut some off from its service and lobbied against other companies’s free alternatives to its A.I.
Over the last year, other technology companies and investors have organized to push back, according to more than 20 people in the technology industry, many of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to preserve their relationships with Anthropic.

title: Inside Microsoft’s Rush to Get Back Online After a Global Outage
rawText:
Supported by
Inside Microsoft’s Rush to Get Back Online After a Global Outage
A prolonged outage left many without email and other services, the most recent reminder that the world’s technological underpinnings rely on just a few companies.
Late into the night Thursday, hundreds of Microsoft engineers and top executives were sitting in their darkened offices or home basements, logged into a video conference triaging a nightmare scenario for a technology company.
The world still runs on email, and much of that is processed through Microsoft Outlook. For hours, a company outage affected hospitals, schools, businesses and Congressional offices in Washington. Even Microsoft’s own staff couldn’t use email.
On the videoconference, Scott Guthrie, the senior most executive overseeing the company’s computing infrastructure, was proposing possible fixes, according to a person familiar with the call who was not authorized to speak publicly. People chewed on fingernails, rubbed their foreheads and debated how to turn off other services to prevent a “stampeding herd” so that as systems come back online, they would not be overwhelmed with new demands and shut back down.
By Friday morning, the company had apologized at least twice. It said it determined that the problem stemmed from a recent upgrade to its network, which shut down some servers, and that the systems were steadily improving. “Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage,” the company said in a statement. “While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration.”
Finally, they had kept the herd at bay.
The prolonged and widespread outage was just the most recent reminder that the technological underpinnings of modern life and business are run through just a handful of major companies. And while cyberattacks and malicious actors can target their systems, sometimes the companies learn the hard way that they can introduce devastating flaws when updating or maintaining their own global systems.
Hospitals, law enforcement and government agencies and other vital services are often left vulnerable — unable to function for hours or days at a time.

title: Wall Street Braces for Anthropic’s Spending
rawText:
Supported by
Wall Street Braces for Anthropic’s Aggressive Spending
The company’s financial picture may get murky as it deals with employee stock compensation and the growing costs of artificial intelligence.
Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, introduced his artificial intelligence company to potential stock market investors this week with a sublime vision. He predicted the end of cancer and mental illness within a decade, and a transformation of cognitive work. “If we do this right, we can create an age of miracles,” he said in a marketing video for Anthropic’s initial public offering.
Wall Street is grappling with how much it may cost to get to utopia.
Stock analysts at Goldman Sachs, the investment bank leading Anthropic’s I.P.O., have told investors privately this week that they forecast the company will burn through more than $65 billion next year, and another $41 billion in 2028, said two people familiar with those discussions. Those totals would make Anthropic’s spending among the most aggressive corporate bets on funding the giant A.I. infrastructure build-out.
“We are in aggressive investment mode,” Krishna Rao, Anthropic’s chief financial officer, said in the video, without discussing specific spending forecasts.
That spending would create a drastically different financial picture than Anthropic has shown recently. The company generated cash from its business in the first nine months of this year, its I.P.O. prospectus shows, a feat in the expensive business of A.I. model development. It has barely spent the $141 billion it raised privately from investors.
The listing on Nasdaq, expected next Thursday, could value Anthropic at $1.4 trillion. It would not only cement its status as one of the world’s most prominent companies but hand it additional firepower to help it pull further ahead of well-heeled rivals like OpenAI and Alphabet. The I.P.O. would deliver Anthropic an additional $100 billion to spend, and make it easier to raise even more money to fund those huge commitments.
But Anthropic’s public debut will lead to costs that don’t appear today. It said in the prospectus it anticipated about $40 billion of expenses in the coming years tied to preexisting stock grants it has given employees that haven’t yet hit its accounting books.

title: Jensen Huang’s Resignation From Nvidia Worries the A.I. Start-Up World
rawText:
Supported by
Silicon Valley Start-Ups Face a Future Without Jensen Huang’s Money
Mr. Huang championed start-ups, with Nvidia holding $48 billion worth of stakes in 229 private companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic, at the end of July.
For years, Jensen Huang was a frequent presence at Silicon Valley start-up events, networking with founders, judging pitch competitions and showing up at “demo” days.
The Nvidia chief executive became a godlike figure in the start-up ecosystem, not just because the industry idolized him as one of the world’s most successful entrepreneurs. Mr. Huang, 63, also made it his mission to help start-ups gain a foothold against the industry’s biggest and most powerful tech companies, providing funding and computing power.
“As many good ideas as we have, you don’t have all the world’s good ideas,” he said on the Acquired podcast in 2023.
So Mr. Huang’s abrupt resignation from Nvidia on Thursday has investors and start-up founders nervous that they have lost a powerful ally.
“Nvidia is the central bank of A.I. and all of a sudden, the Fed chairman is out,” said Tomasz Tunguz, an investor at Theory Ventures, which funds young start-ups.
Nvidia held $48 billion worth of stakes in 229 private companies, including large stakes in OpenAI and Anthropic, at the end of July, according to securities filings. It more than doubled its start-up investments in six months.

title: China rules out hosting Cop33 climate summit in 2028
rawText:
China has ruled out hosting the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of deliberations, leaving the field open for other Asian countries to hold it, the Guardian understands.
The decision will disappoint many countries and climate experts, who had hoped the world’s biggest emitter would take the lead on the global stage, as the US under Donald Trump has vacated all forms of international cooperation on the climate.
Al Gore, the former US vice-president, was among those left disheartened by the decision. “I would be very much in favour of that idea [of China hosting the summit],” he told the Guardian. “It’s too bad.”
China is in the midst of an economic transformation, from being heavily dependent on coal to becoming an “electro state”. John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, told the Guardian that China was leaving the rest of the world behind in forging and using the low-carbon technologies of the future.
Renewable energy generation capacity has now outstripped coal in China, and its greenhouse gas emissions appear to have declined slightly this year.
Sales of electric vehicles in the country have also taken off, making up nearly two-thirds of the market last month, and China’s clean energy industries drove more than 90% of the country’s investment growth last year.
The rules of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) mean an Asian country should host in 2028.
Gareth Redmond-King, the international lead at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank, said China’s position as an industrial powerhouse would have made it a formidable contender to hold the summit.
“It would undoubtedly be significant for the world’s biggest emitter and second-biggest economy to host a climate Cop,” he said.
“They’re leading the world on investment, manufacture and deployment of clean energy tech, and their emissions have started to tick down. As a leadership story, China hosting Cop33 would be a big deal.”
It is not clear why China has decided against hosting the conference, but several experts that spoke to the Guardian suggested that the US electoral cycle was likely to have been a factor. The next US presidential election will take place on 7 November 2028, and Cop33 is scheduled for 6 to 17 November that year.
After the strong showing by Democrats in the recent midterm elections, in which voter concern over the climate crisis was thought to be a factor, the Democrats will be hoping to elect a climate-friendly president in 2028. But even if they succeed, Trump will still be in office until the following January.
The US president rejects climate science and withdrew the US from the Paris agreement, and is also withdrawing from its parent treaty, the 1992 UNFCCC.
China seeks to be seen as a leader among developing countries, but has been wary of stepping into the gap left by the US. Under the Democratic presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama, the US and China enjoyed a close partnership on climate issues, setting joint targets on reducing methane and developing clean technology.
Cop33 will be an important meeting because it will include the “global stocktake” – a mechanism under the 2015 Paris climate agreement that examines countries’ progress on cutting emissions in line with the goal of limiting global temperature rises to 1.5C.
That limit is now certain to be surpassed, but experts say countries should now try to minimise the temperature “overshoot”, to avoid worse ravages from extreme weather.
India’s government considered offering to host Cop33 for several months earlier this year, but also decided against it. India’s coal use has been increasing, even as the country exceeds its own renewable energy targets.
The Guardian understands that other countries mulling a bid to host Cop33 include Uzbekistan, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand.

title: Microsoft’s Outlook email hit by new outage
rawText:
Microsoft said its Outlook email service is currently experiencing an outage, preventing users from accessing their inboxes.
The issue was initially flagged as affecting the U.S. and the Americas, and later expanded to affect “any region.”
Microsoft hasn’t given a specific cause, but said that it was providing updates in its admin center, which wasn’t reachable at the time of publication. In a post on X for users who can’t access the admin center, Microsoft said some of its infrastructure was experiencing “elevated load,” and that it was “redistributing connection traffic across our broader worldwide infrastructure to help balance the load.”
The company’s last major incident was in September, when a days-long outage hit Microsoft 365, its online productivity suite that includes Outlook. During that outage, Microsoft blamed a “core authentication configuration” issue that prevented users from accessing the service.
It’s unclear to what extent the outage extends to other services. TechCrunch will reach out to Microsoft for comment, as soon as our email service has resumed.

title: Thursday briefing: What we do (and don’t) know about Alice Huang and the Nvidia affair
rawText:
Good morning. Espionage is supposed to be a secretive business, and spies are supposed to be virtually invisible. That hasn’t been the case for Alice Huang, the mysterious Shanghai executive who formed a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang, the founder of Nvidia, one of America’s most powerful tech companies.
Many questions have arisen since it emerged that US intelligence believes that Huang (no relation of Jensen’s) is an asset recruited by the Chinese intelligence services to spy on behalf of Beijing. This morning’s newsletter explains what we know about the story, and what it tells us about the effectiveness of Chinese espionage. That’s after the headlines.
Five big stories
- UK | Ministers are considering changing the law to force the entertainment industry to better protect women and children in the wake of the revelations over David Walliams and the conviction of Russell Brand.
- Climate | The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country.
- US midterms | Democrat Scott Colom has become the first Black senator in Mississippi to be elected since Reconstruction, in a stunning upset after more than a week of vote counting in one of the country’s most reliably red states.
- Europe | Millions of people across Spain have joined the country’s first general strike in 14 years, setting up picket lines to protest against soaring housing prices before an election in which the far right could be catapulted into power.
- Technology | Police officers risk arresting innocent people, especially from ethnic minorities, if they treat inaccurate facial recognition data as evidence, an official report has found.
In depth: Everything we know (or don’t) about the Nvidia affair
Last month, the New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had formed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, the former executive of a Singapore-based computing company, Megaspeed. Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia; it buys the extremely valuable chips they produce, which are essential for powering AI, and rents computing space to Chinese companies. The US government had already been investigating whether Megaspeed could be flouting US restrictions and smuggling chips into China – allegations that both Nvidia and Megaspeed deny.
US intelligence officials, who had been conducting surveillance on Alice Huang, eventually concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset who had been passing on information to Beijing. The intelligence behind this assessment is classified, so we don’t know exactly what they found – or which intelligence body was conducting the surveillance. Nvidia said Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected”, but on Sunday, Huang admitted in a letter to his employees that he had been having an affair. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children,” he said, adding that he was “deeply sorry”.
Nvidia’s valuation is inextricably linked to Huang. By yesterday, $430bn (5.5%) had been wiped off its share price, and in the early hours of this morning, that figure ballooned to about $600bn following reports that Nvidia’s board was deciding whether to oust Huang (you can follow the latest on that here). The company has appointed outside counsel to review the pair’s relationship and says it has no reason to believe that secrets or national security were compromised.
The most interesting aspects of this story are the questions we can’t (yet) answer. Did Nvidia’s board know that US intelligence suspected Alice Huang was a spy? What evidence led US intelligence to conclude she was spying for China? What information could she have passed to Beijing? And …
Who is Alice Huang?
Reporters and sleuths on Chinese social media have been trying to get to the bottom of who the Megaspeed chief really is. On Tuesday, the Financial Times published an interesting report (£) about Alice Huang

title: Jensen Huang Said to Have Had Relationship With Nvidia Executive Who Reports to Him
rawText:
Supported by
Jensen Huang Said to Have Had Relationship With Nvidia Executive Who Reports to Him
Mr. Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, is already facing scrutiny over an affair with a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence determined was a Chinese spy.
Jensen Huang, the leader of Nvidia who is under investigation for an affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence determined is a Chinese spy, also had an extramarital relationship with an executive who reports to him, according to five people who worked at the company.
The relationship, which has not been previously reported, was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, said the people, who spoke under the condition of anonymity to describe sensitive information. Under Nvidia’s code of conduct, employees are told to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict” including “personal relationships,” and the company states that it “promptly investigates reports of misconduct.” Many corporations have policies against managers having relationships with subordinates.
Mr. Huang, 63, and Ms. Powell, 48, were captured on video being affectionate at a San Jose, Calif., hotel during a Nvidia conference in March, according to two of the people who worked at the company. The New York Times has not seen the video.
Both Mr. Huang and Ms. Powell are married to other people.
Mr. Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has turned it into the premier supplier of artificial intelligence chips, has been under intensifying scrutiny. Last month, The Times reported that a Chinese executive he had become close to had been identified by U.S. officials as a Chinese intelligence asset.
This month, after Mr. Huang acknowledged the affair, Nvidia’s board opened an investigation into the matter that is being led by the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. The Republican leaders of three influential House committees have also asked Mr. Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with the woman, who goes by the name Alice Huang.
China has denied the espionage claims. Ms. Huang, the Chinese executive accused of spying for Beijing, has not responded to requests for comment.

title: Nvidia Scandal Puts Lori Huang, Jensen Huang’s Wife, In the Spotlight
rawText:
Supported by
Jensen Huang’s Affair Puts His Wife in the Spotlight
Lori Huang, who has been married to the Nvidia chief executive for more than 40 years, stands out among tech titan spouses for how private she has been.
In November 2021, Jensen Huang attended the annual dinner held by the Semiconductor Industry Association in San Jose, Calif. That night, the trade group gave Mr. Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia, its highest honor, named for the Intel co-founder Robert Noyce.
Mr. Huang arrived early with his wife, Lori Huang, and quickly headed to the bar at the pre-dinner reception, saying the event was the first time he had been out of his house since the Covid lockdown began in March 2020. He introduced Ms. Huang to reporters who clustered nearby, but they mainly talked to him.
By the time Mr. Huang received the award, two hours had passed. The Nvidia leader walked onstage with a bottle of red wine and two glasses, sharing them with a moderator and taking the conversation into unexpected topics. Throughout, Ms. Huang remained in the background.
For more than 40 years, Ms. Huang has been by Mr. Huang’s side as he built his fledgling chip start-up into one of the most valuable companies in the world. Nvidia’s success turned Mr. Huang into an international business star. His face is on sweaters, his signature leather jackets have become collectors items, and his net worth has soared to nearly $150 billion.
By contrast, Ms. Huang stayed far from the spotlight.
That changed this week, when Mr. Huang, 63, revealed he had an affair with an executive identified by the U.S. government as a Chinese spy. In his admission, which he shared in a message to Nvidia employees, Mr. Huang apologized to his wife, as well as his two children, who both work at Nvidia, thrusting them into the limelight.
The bombshell news had implications for U.S. national security and the economy. Nvidia’s role as the A.I. industry’s main supplier of chips makes Mr. Huang a crucial linchpin for an industry that has come to dominate the stock market.

title: El Supremo rechaza suspender también el voto de los hijos de los nacionalizados por la ‘ley de nietos’
rawText:
El Supremo rechaza suspender también el voto de los hijos de los nacionalizados por la ‘ley de nietos’
Los magistrados desestiman la petición de Vox y de Iustitia Europa por el “breve lapso temporal” que queda hasta las elecciones del 29-N
Los hijos de los españoles nacionalizados por la ley de nietos que vivan en el extranjero podrán votar el 29-N. El Tribunal Supremo ha renunciado a extender a este grupo la suspensión del derecho al sufragio que decretó en septiembre para los hijos y nietos de la emigración y el exilio que han obtenido la nacionalidad con la Ley de Memoria Democrática. Los magistrados han rechazado la petición de Iustitia Europa y de Vox, que reclamaron que la medida adoptada por los jueces para más de 163.000 nacionalizados como descendientes del exilio se extendiera a su vez a los hijos de estos, nacionalizados por otro apartado de la Ley de Memoria que no está afectado por la suspensión del voto acordada por el Supremo. La Abogacía del Estado se había opuesto a esa posibilidad y alegó que ampliar la suspensión del derecho al voto pondría en riesgo el cumplimiento de los trámites legales para el 29-N e incluso podría afectar al escrutinio. El tribunal coincide en que es demasiado “breve” el “lapso temporal” que queda hasta los comicios, por lo que opta por no ampliar la suspensión del voto. No obstante, en otra resolución notificada este martes, los jueces insisten en que los últimos datos aportados por el Gobierno acrecientan “los indicios racionales de presuntas irregularidades de gran relevancia en la configuración” del censo de españoles en el extranjero.
Los magistrados recalcan que la petición se planteó una vez “transcurrido más de la mitad del periodo electoral, a una semana del comienzo de la campaña” y a dos semanas del inicio del depósito del voto en urna en los consulados de los nacionalizados que viven en el extranjero. En este sentido, entienden que iniciar ahora un proceso de revisión del Censo Electoral de Residentes Ausentes (CERA) ―“además de los interrogantes que suscita la posibilidad material de ejecución efectiva en el breve lapso temporal existente hasta la fecha de votación y de su escrutinio”― resulta “contrario a las exigencias derivadas de los principios de seguridad jurídica y de estabilidad electoral”.
El tribunal insiste en que las decisiones que ha adoptado hasta ahora sobre los nietos “han partido y están presididas por la necesidad de garantizar la seguridad jurídica, concretada en la pureza o certeza del censo electoral que debería aplicarse a los procesos electorales”. Y recalca que el pasado septiembre, cuando suspendió el voto de los nacionalizados que viven en el extranjero, el escenario nacional no incluía un horizonte electoral inminente.
El Supremo ordenó en septiembre excluir del censo a más de 163.000 españoles que adquirieron la nacionalidad bajo el paraguas del apartado 1.1. de la disposición adicional octava de la Ley de Memoria, que reconoce el derecho a la nacionalidad, entre otros, a los hijos y nietos de quienes la hubieran perdido tras haberse exiliado por razones políticas, ideológicas o de orientación sexual. Pero esa decisión dejó dentro del censo a los hijos de quienes tienen el voto suspendido y que se han nacionalizado gracias a ellos. Estos últimos han adquirido también la nacionalidad por dicha ley, pero por otro apartado, el 1.b de la disposición adicional octava. Sobre este grupo es sobre el que se había reclamado que se extendiera la suspensión del voto. Según los datos aportados por Exteriores, hay 189.678 españoles nacionalizados por esta vía incluidos en el CERA del 1 de agosto, el que cuenta para las elecciones del 29-N, pero esta cifra incluye también a los hijos de quienes obtuvieron la nacionalidad por la Ley de Memoria Histórica de 2007, que no está bajo la lupa del alto tribunal.

title: Uyghurs facing deportation by Thailand say they will be ‘like slaves’ in China
rawText:
The deportation of two more Uyghurs to China from Thailand would put their lives in grave danger, activists have said, with one of the men saying he would be “like a slave” if he was sent back.
Last year, Thai authorities forcibly deported 40 Uyghur men to China despite pleas from the men themselves and the UN.
 
The US and Canada had reportedly offered to resettle them, but Bangkok appeared to want to avoid upsetting Beijing. The UN has said the returnees’ whereabouts remain unknown.
Now, two more men fear becoming the latest victims of Beijing’s repressive crackdown against the largely Muslim ethnic group, condemned by the UN as a potential crime against humanity.
The girlfriend of one of the men said her boyfriend, whose name is being withheld for security reasons, told the Guardian he wanted to go “anywhere else but China”.
Human rights groups said two Uyghur men were at risk of deportation after recently being transferred to an immigration detention centre and they feared Thai authorities may once again give in to pressure from Beijing.
Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch, called for the men to be allowed to travel to a safe third country. “Previous Thai governments have kept Uyghurs in inhumane detention for years and then complied with Beijing’s demands to send them to China, where they were forcibly disappeared,” she said.
The men had been serving a seven-year prison sentence for offences related to an attempted escape from immigration detention in January 2020. They were part of a group of more than 200 Uyghur men, women and children who were apprehended by Thai police in 2014 near the border with Malaysia after they fled from China.
Since 2014, women and children in the group have been released to Turkey, while the men have been deported to China, in separate batches, attracting criticism from the United Nations and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio.
Uyghurs, a Turkic minority mainly from the Xinjiang region in China, have been subjected to decades of oppressive and discriminatory treatment from the Chinese authorities. This has included the incarceration of hundreds of thousands of people in detention camps aimed at stamping out their cultural identity.
Beijing has defended its policies in Xinjiang as being aimed at poverty alleviation and counter-terrorism.
In July, Marzeyya Kasem’s (who asked to be referred to by her Islamic alias) boyfriend wrote to her in a letter that he would be “like a slave” if he was sent back to China. “Sometimes I thought why I’m a human being. What I do wrong against China … no want to go back to China,” he wrote. She shared the letter with a Thai rights group.
The two men facing imminent deportation reportedly pleaded their case to Thailand’s office of the National Human Rights Commission on Wednesday.
Relatives of Uyghurs have said the Chinese government was “paranoid about Uyghurs going to a safe country in large numbers and living together”, and preferred to have them deported.
It is not clear whether China has issued a formal extradition request for the two men. But Chaipruak Doungprapat, Thailand’s national security council chief, told reporters that the men, along with three other Uyghurs who are still in prison, had arrest warrants outstanding in China.
Some have questioned whether criminal warrants could be credible considering that at least one of them, Kasem’s boyfriend, was a minor when he left China. “If they are really wanted for a crime in China, why didn’t China immediately issue a [Interpol] red notice [when they were detained in 2014]?” asked Kasem.
Kasem believes that because Thailand was criticised for last year’s mass deportation, this time the authorities were trying to establish a more credible legal basis for the move.

title: NZ election 2026: New Zealand faces weeks of uncertainty with results ‘too close to call’
rawText:
New Zealand could be facing a weeks-long wait to know the shape of its next government, after its nail-biting election failed to hand a decisive victory to either the incumbent rightwing coalition or opposition left bloc.
On preliminary results, the centre-right National party, led by the prime minister, Christopher Luxon, managed to secure enough seats to govern alongside its traditional coalition partners, the libertarian Act and populist New Zealand First parties.
But with some seats won by very slim margins, and special votes yet to be counted, that success is precarious, resulting in an election too close to call until official results are released on 27 November.
Special votes include overseas votes and ballots cast outside a voter’s electorate. In 2023, 600,000 such votes were made, 21% of the total. These votes tend to favour the left – in 2023, special votes resulted in Te Pāti Māori (the Māori party) and the Greens gaining three seats between them.
With nearly 100% of the regular votes counted on Saturday night, National secured 42 seats, Act 13 and New Zealand First 12. The combined 67-seat majority is wafer thin, with the left bloc just three seats behind.
Speaking to a room full of the party faithful at Auckland’s Viaduct events centre just before midnight, Luxon said the results were “too close to call” and the special votes would need to be counted before negotiations could begin.
National was still the largest party in parliament, he said, and had “a pathway to forming the next government”. National pipped Labour by 0.02% in the party vote.
Labour, led by Chris Hipkins, secured 35 seats, while its traditional coalition partners the Greens won 16 and Te Pāti Māori five. Even with the seven seats from the centrist newcomer party, Opportunity, the left bloc is three seats short of forming a government.
Before a rowdy crowd of supporters at the Cosmopolitan Club in Upper Hutt, north of Wellington, Hipkins joked that New Zealand had spoken but “it may take a bit longer to work out what they’ve said”.
“As things stand tonight, it is clear that we are not going to know the shape of our next government for a little while longer yet,” Hipkins said, promising that Labour would get “straight to work” should the final count land in its favour.
The collapse of the two major parties, amid a sluggish economy and stubbornly high inflation, is feeding record support for the smaller parties, including Act, New Zealand First and the Greens. It is also helped propel Opportunity into parliament for the first time.
Opinion polls in the lead-up to the election had Opportunity placed to become the kingmaker. At this stage, the right bloc does not need the party to govern, but if special votes change the landscape, its predicted role could come to fruition.
Currently at 5.9%, the centrist party has met the threshold needed to enter parliament, a historic first. Since New Zealand adopted the mixed-member proportional (MMP) electoral system in 1996, no new party has been able to meet that threshold – all the other minor parties have been born from MPs or groups splintering from larger parties.
The party’s leader, Qiulae Wong, told her supporters in Auckland she was “stoked”.
“It’s looking very promising for us,” she said. “Let’s just see how the rest of the votes fall.”
In New Zealand, voters cast two votes: one for an electorate MP and one for a party. The system is meant to produce a parliament that reflects each party’s share of the nationwide vote.
However, if New Zealanders vote for more electorate MPs from a particular party than their party vote would entitle them to, they get to keep the extra MPs in what is called an overhang.
National won more seats that its party support allows for, meaning it could gain an extra five seats to make up the balance.

title: Israel's president taps opposition candidate, not Netanyahu, to form a government
rawText:
Israel's president taps opposition candidate, not Netanyahu, to form a government
Israel's president has tapped Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's main political rival, Gadi Eisenkot, to try to form the next government. It's a setback for Netanyahu, whose party won the most seats but failed to secure a parliamentary majority.
Netanyahu's Likud party won 27 seats in last month's election, six more than Eisenkot's Yashar party. But neither secured enough support to command a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament.
President Isaac Herzog will formally give Eisenkot the mandate at 5 p.m. local time on Sunday.
Eisenkot is a former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, serving as the country's top military commander from 2015 to 2019. A veteran of several military campaigns, he later joined Netanyahu's emergency war cabinet following the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel, but left the following year, accusing Netanyahu of failing to make progress toward ending the Gaza war and securing the release of hostages. Eisenkot lost his son, Gal, a reservist killed in Gaza, as well as two nephews during the war.
Eisenkot leads the centrist Yashar party, which he founded on an anti-corruption and government reform platform. He will now have 28 days to put together a coalition government, with a possible 14-day extension.
That gives him up to six weeks to negotiate with rival parties and secure the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.
If Eisenkot fails, Herzog can give another lawmaker a chance to form a government. If those efforts also fail, Israel could face another election. Netanyahu would remain caretaker prime minister in the meantime.

title: The ‘slam dunk’ that wasn’t: Promising cholesterol drug fails to prevent heart attacks or stroke
rawText:
An experimental drug that held great promise in driving down a dangerous form of cholesterol didn’t show any measurable impact on heart attack or stroke in a clinical trial. The failure of the Novartis drug pelacarsen to help people who have high levels of lipoprotein(a) stunned researchers, who called it a massive blow to preventive cardiology.
Results of the clinical trial of pelacarsen, an injection, presented Saturday at a meeting of the American Heart Association, found there were zero decreases in stroke, heart attack, cardiovascular deaths or the number of procedures to open blocked arteries or restore blood flow to the heart.
“I really thought that this was going to be a slam dunk,” said Dr. Amanda Doran, an assistant professor of medicine in the division of cardiovascular medicine at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. Vanderbilt was one of nearly 800 sites involved in the clinical trial, called Horizon. “We were pretty invested, so it obviously hurts.”
Pelacarsen targets a stealthy and particularly lethal form of cholesterol called lipoprotein(a), or Lp(a). Much like low-density lipoprotein — LDL, or the “bad” cholesterol — Lp(a) causes plaque to build up in arteries. But it also helps form blood clots, and unlike LDL, it is entirely genetic.
About 1 in 5 Americans have high Lp(a), according to the American Heart Association. Most don’t realize they’re at risk.
Because people are born with those high levels, diet and exercise have no effect. That’s why heart experts have been so keen to find a drug that would handle the problem.
The Horizon trial included 8,322 people with high Lp(a) levels and who’d already had a heart attack, stroke or other heart problem within 10 years of starting the trial.
The drug did reduce Lp(a) significantly, by 78%, compared to a placebo drug that cut levels by 13%.
But that huge reduction ultimately meant nothing in terms of cardiovascular health.
Dr. Steven Nissen, the chief academic officer of the Heart, Vascular & Thoracic Institute at the Cleveland Clinic, led the trial. He said the dismal results took him by “extreme surprise.”
“Everybody, me included, believed that lowering levels of lipoprotein(a) substantially would reduce the risk of major cardiovascular events,” he said. “There is simply no evidence here that people that got more reduction did better.”
The findings, also published Saturday in the New England Journal of Medicine, confounded Nissen and other cardiologists who’ve long known that controlling other markers of heart health — LDL and blood pressure, for example — provides clear benefits.
“I have not seen a more shockingly neutral trial in a while,” said Dr. Karol Watson, co-director of the UCLA Program in Preventive Cardiology and a professor at UCLA’s David Geffen School of Medicine. Watson was not involved with the research.
There are several theories as to why the drug didn’t work as anticipated. It’s possible, Watson said, that the therapy was given too late in life to make a difference. The average age of Horizon’s study participants was 60, and they were followed for an average of five years.

“Remember that Lp(a) is a genetic disorder, so from the time a baby’s conceived, their Lp(a) is high. If we just swooped in in the last five years, maybe that’s too late,” Watson said.
Study participants were also treated aggressively in other ways to drive down their LDL cholesterol and get blood pressure readings into a healthy range. Participants may have also been taking aspirin because of a history of heart attack or stroke, which could have lessened Lp(a)’s clotting risk.
“How much of the Lp(a)-associated risk was remaining? We just don’t know,” Watson said.
Does Lp(a) still matter as a marker of heart health?
